IS BOLSHEVISM POSSIBLE
IN KWANGTUNG?

TSE YING-PAK'S ACTIVITIES

Main Soviet Theories Unacceptable; The
Attitude Of Labour

So much has been heard of
late of the possibility of
Bolshevism being given a trial in
Kwangtung, that a "Hongkong
Telegraph" representative who
recently visited Canton took the
opportunity of enquiring into the
situation, seeking information
chiefly in Labour circles. The
following impressions which he
formed may be found of in-
terest at the moment:—

Strictly speaking, there is no
Labour Party in Kwangtung in
the sense in which the term is
understood politically in other
countries. On the political side
the aims of labour have in
recent years been expressed the
Kuomintang Party, which funda-
mentally is a republican
organization, and purports to
represent the three great
divisions of the people—the
workers, the farmers and the
professionals. On the economic
side, the various Labour Guilds
have formed a more potential
factor, and have not hesitated
to usurp functions which pro-
perly belong to the Kuomintang.
One explanation of this is to be
found in the plurality of posts
filled by members of both
organizations. A noteworthy
example is furnished by the
case of Tse Ying-pak, who,
whilst being a prominent mem-
ber of the Kuomintang and also
the Provincial Parliament, ex-
ercises also a large influence
over some two hundred Labour
Guilds.

Aiming At Unity

Of late a number of similar
or allied institutions have been
founded in Kwangtung, and the
action of one of them, the
"Canton Rehabilitation Society,"
now tends to bring about a
closer fusion of interests between
the Kuomintang and the Labour
Guilds. Tse Ying-pak refers to
this new organization variously
as the Reconstruction, Repres-
entative or Educational Society.
Broadly speaking, the principal
aim is to solidify public opinion
in the province with a view to
preserving its unity which lately
has been much undermined by
the internal political strife.

With all the complexities
which are to be found in Chin-
ese politics, it is difficult for the
observer to ascertain to what
extent, the teachings of Karl
Marx, as propounded by his
disciple, Tse Ying-pak, have ob-
tained a hold on the mass of
Chinese workers. But, however
ignorant the average Chinese
workers are of the economic as-
pect of the doctrine, their leader,
Tse Ying-pak, has at any rate
a clear idea of the work he has
been engaged on for quite a
number of years now. It is
interesting to note that this
man, who was a Queen's College
student and in his early years
had taught as a master at St.
Paul's College, was one forced
to flee the country as a political
refugee to escape the wrath of
the Manchus. Since then he has
taken up Socialism seriously.
He, in fact, became such a
strong convert to it that he felt
himself impelled to establish
schools at Shanghai, where the
curriculum had aimed chiefly at
the training of young minds for
the reception of the principles
of Socialism. His more recent
activities have been directed
with special emphasis to the
merchants of the Kwangtung
province, and such propaganda
as he has caused to be inserted
in the numerous papers under
his control give unmistakable
evidence of his antagonism to
the capitalist class as a whole.
During the big seamen's strike
in Hongkong he played an im-
portant part as a prominent
Guild leader.

In Tse Ying-pak, Dr. Sun has
a powerful worker whose in-
fluence over the mass of labour-
ers is now being utilized in
shaping events to his own
purpose. It was not mere im-
pulse that recently led Tse to
address his open appeal on the
Customs dispute to Congress and
the American people. A fact
which may not be generally
known is that he is a member
of the American Socialist Party
—the first Chinese to be ad-
mitted into membership and he
has been in touch with the
activities of that section of
political thought in America.

I had the opportunity of meet-
ing him the other day during the
interval in which he sought
respite from his work in the
"Executive department of the
Kuomintang" temporarily hous-
ed on the Bund, to take a cup
of tea at a restaurant. The cares
of Labour had rested on his
shoulders very lightly, and I
was surprised to see a man of
jovial appearance with a marked
rotundity of figure. The occasion
was a party participated in by
a number of young men whom
he indicated, with a wave of his
hands, as being "students."
On that and subsequent oc-
casions when I came into
contact with him it was of
particular interest to note the
marked deference shown to him
by other men on the party.
Of this there can be no doubt
—that Tse Ying-pak exercises
an extensive influence in political
circles at Canton.

Bolshevism Not Favoured

I asked him if there were any
truth in the persistent reports
that Bolshevism was being ad-
opted in Canton, and he replied
in the negative, stating that the
principal aim of Sovietism was
not accepted by the organization
of which he had control, al-
though certain details were ac-
cepted. Speaking of the recent
visit of a Soviet delegate to
Canton, this Labour leader said
that the envoy submitted a
translation of the chief tenets of
Bolshevism, but that whilst
accepting some of these, the
main essence was found to be
inapplicable to Kwangtung. The
Labour ideal in Kwangtung at
the moment was expressed as
consolidation of the rights of the
three divisions of labour in the
country, but the Kuomintang
aspires to a higher plane—that
of unity of China and of her five
principal races—Chinese, Man-
chus, Mongolians, Tibetans and
the tribes of Turkestan; and the
elimination of racial hatred in
all matters, political and
economic. Such are the impres-
sions left on me after having
taken considerable pains to as-
certain to what degree Labour
in South China is tending to-
wards Socialism in its political
activities.

The Central-China Post
Friday, November 23, 1923.

LENIN

We used to receive from the Shanghai publishers a Weekly Review called “The New Russia” which was evidently issued in the interests of the Soviet Government. Then it ceased to turn up, and we supposed it had gone under having found its task too great for it. This was nothing less, according to its motto than: “The Revival of the World through Russia.” But once more we have received a copy and it is the “Anniversary Issue.” Here’s luck, we thought, we shall now have an account of the year’s progress in Russia, and a cheering description of the present situation in all departments. Instead of this it proved that, out of its ten articles, nine were devoted to the glorification of Lenin and one to Karakhan.

There were four full-page portraits—one of Lenin at the age of three, one of Lenin as a Middle School boy before he was expelled, one of Lenin convalescing after being shot, and one of the present day Lenin. The letter-press was so offensive with its fulsome adulation, as to raise ones gorge. It is hard to imagine any disinterested person reading this Review unless a fee was paid for the task. There is practically no brass-tacks information given even about Lenin, but an abundance of high-sounding words that may mean anything or nothing. It recalled to our mind the story of King Herod who, arrayed in his royal robes and sitting on his throne, made an oration to the people with such effect that they acclaimed him by shouting: “It is the voice of a god and not of a man”. Then, we read: “Immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, and he was eaten up of worms and gave up the ghost.” Lenin as here described is ripe for the smiting, and if the angel would only appear again, there would be no lack of persons ready to call in the worms.

We take it that this Review does not rely for its support on the Russians in Shanghai, since most of them are there because they have no love for Lenin; and we cannot conceive that any non-Russian would pay a cent for it. Where the money comes from neither editor nor publisher is likely to tell us, but we will not be far wrong in supposing that the Soviet Government supplies the funds. To all intents and purposes Lenin is that Government, so it means he must be busy in Shanghai raising a monument to himself at his own expense. This beats the late Mr. Carnegie, who used his super-abundant wealth to erect monuments to himself in the shape of Carnegie Libraries and Carnegie Organs on condition that other people kept them up for all time coming. In Lenin’s case when the cash stops the monument will disappear. This indicates a strain of vanity in the great man that makes him a very little man indeed.

And what did Lenin really do for Russia? The Review does not claim that he did very much; all the credit is given to the peasants and the workers. “It was the peasants and the workers—who through their tenacity and energy overthrew the capitalist world. By their

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS. MONDAY. JULY 30, 1923.

SHANGHAI, JULY 30, 1923.

BOLSHEVISM IN CHINA

Close and reliable investigation tends to indicate that the propaganda campaign—of which papers in Japan have recently made mention—to spread the seeds of Bolshevism in China is not by any means finding the ground too stony. That very large sums of money and that numerous very able propagandists are being used in the work is certain, and it is also known that considerable headway is being made in such districts as Canton, Hankow, Tientsin, Peking, and in the western Provinces. All the tricks of the trade—which became so familiar to European nations during the war—are being employed and, of course, so long as money is forthcoming the agents of Russia will experience but little difficulty in securing native apostles willing and anxious to preach the gospel to their countrymen. While M. Joffe was in Shanghai recently, he had one or two conversations with Dr. Sun Yat-sen, but it is now thought that the Canton leader has discovered excellent reasons why his influence should be directed against the campaign, or, at least, why he should in no way lend his support to the movement. It is unfortunate that it still seems quite impossible to secure dependable information as to how the system is working in Russia itself but a very fair barometer—and one which a people such as the Chinese may be relied upon to gauge fairly accurately—is the continued influx of Russian refugees to China and their very evident determination to live on, even in extremely difficult conditions, in China or elsewhere rather than return to the country of their birth.

While the gentle plausibilities of the propagandist may thus to some extent be overridden, the important fact must not be overlooked that the soil for his work in several important districts of China is of a very fertile nature. The terrible tragedy of continued misgovernment of the people by Peking and the provincial authorities is a stepping stone of which the fullest advantage will certainly be taken by Bolshevik agents, and not a few close judges of the situation are inclined to think that, unless some radical change is made by the authorities, Chinese or foreign, the possibility of an important Bolshevik success in the Far East ere long is not altogether to be contemptuously dismissed. Certainly there is a very strong argument in the statement that any form of government would be better than the present helplessness of Peking, and as it is believed the Bolshevik propagandists now arm themselves with the very welcome additional slogan of "End the armies and end war," the creed is one which is making a wider and wider appeal. In the Canton district, it is known that professed supporters, members of well-known societies, are numbered by thousands, and there is reason to believe the authorities there are not at all easy about the situation. Fortunately, although Shanghai is also, of course, a centre the authorities are to be congratulated upon the close and careful supervision which has been exercised. This has undoubtedly had the desired effect and although the work continues, the successful efforts which have been made against several of the Chinese emissaries have served as a hint to their colleagues. The Chinese postal authorities, too, are to be congratulated on the success of their counter-move in refusing to transmit certain well-known Bolshevik journals through the post. This is useful work and it would be of great assistance if this field of resistance could be developed. The postal authorities, we know, are not overburdened with spare time but the thanks of all true friends of China would be due to them if some extension of this work could be undertaken. The local Chinese authorities, it is satisfactory to know, are fully alive to the situation and in the interest of peace may be depended upon to spare neither time nor pains towards the end in view.

The question of the inauguration of work among Russian refugees who are themselves opposed to Bolshevism is undoubtedly a very delicate one and it may be that the time is scarcely opportune for the consideration of such plans. There are many Russians in our midst who, with a much more intimate knowledge of the fruits of Bolshevism than most of us, regard the propaganda campaign as a distinct menace; but circumstances are such that for the present their close co-operation is a matter of difficulty. Meanwhile, we would again point to the danger confronting the Shanghai district in the attempts being made to house the Chinese Parliament locally. It is sincerely to be hoped that these will be fruitless: and the close attention of the authorities should be energetically directed towards frustration of the attempt. As a panacea for all the evils the Republic has fallen heir to, well-paid Bolshevism would doubtless appeal to quite a few parliamentarians. We have in these days more trouble than enough of our own without the addition of all the plotting and intriguing which appear to occupy the greater part of the time of China's Members of Parliament and the farther away from Shanghai the Chinese Houses of Parliament are maintained the better will this district be pleased.

                the purpose of sowing Bolshevist seeds in China, finds a very
                favourable ground". And again: "There is no doubt that huge sums
                of money are being spent and numerous very experienced propagan-
                dists sent out. It is well known that their propaganda is also
                successful in Canton, Hankow, Tientsin, Peking and in the Western
                Provinces".
                "We cannot argue against this, the "North China Daily News"
                which is making use of someone's "most reliable investigation"
                is an expert in this matter.
                But having undertaken the task of investigating "Bolshevism
                in China" we cannot let the matter rest with the above. Another
                side of the question is likewise of interest viz: what is the
                attitude of foreigners to "facts" related.
                Here once again the "North China Daily News" gives extremely
                valuable suggestions. Having frightened its readers and itself
                the newspaper makes the following propositions:
                I. Counter-propaganda. a) To draw attention of the Chinese
                to the effect that the "whites" thrown out of Russia are making
                their escape into China, where they live in bad conditions, but
                will not return to Russia.
                This in the opinion of the newspaper, must serve as a founda-
                tion for counter-propaganda.
                II. To institute a close watch on propaganda. For this purpose
                the newspaper approves that the Chinese Post Office refuses to
                send out Bolshevik newspapers and journals and suggests:
                That action be taken amongst Russian refugees who oppose Bol-
                shevism, They know very well the results of propaganda and it
                would be well to obtain their co-operation in the matter of
                fighting against Bolshevist propaganda. These measures are certain-
                ly very radical.
                The fact that traitors have fled from Russia and cannot return
                there, is very remarkable considering the terrible results of
                Bolshevism. As regards, however, the proposal to obtain the co-opera-
                tion of the "whites" in opposing Bolshevism, this is still more ra-
                dical suggestion. The majority of them have good experience in
                reconnoitring and their services may be of very great value indeed.
                In the absence of censorship the decisive action of the Post
                Office is a very successful method of struggle.
                Why then not go further and give the initiative to private per-
                sons? If any foreigner sees a journal or a newspaper of Bolshevist
                nature, or if he suspects some person of Bolshevism, he should also
                act. All these propositions of the esteemed British newspaper are
                very good. Only it seems to us that they are wrongly directed. What
                do they matter to ordinary mortals? Would it not be better to sug-
                gest them directly to the authorities. The British semi-official
                newspaper in the role of practical adviser on the matter of strug-
                gling against propaganda proves indeed worthy of its author. Thank
                goodness that this is possible in China. In England, however, it is
                much stricter in this respect.
